title: The Six Trillion Dollar Man
text:
The Six Trillion Dollar Man

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 24 Nov 2026

On Monday, we witnessed Beat Notz’s dictum at work (see War—What Is It Good For?). By now, everyone and their dog should be convinced that the north star of US policymaking is first and foremost to keep US equity prices high. Of course, to anyone paying attention, that much had already been made clear upon President Donald Trump’s signing this June, in Versailles, of the memorandum of understanding with Iran. As soon as he had capped his pen, Donald Trump famously turned to his host, President Emmanuel Macron, and said, “stocks up, oil down” (see The Ceasefire And Mad Markets). A clear signal, if ever there was one, that anyone involved in a conflict with the US should not bother trying to blow up battleships or jet planes, but should instead focus on blowing up the Nasdaq; major equity losses being far more likely to affect US policy than the loss of military assets and soldiers.It is said that there are no atheists in foxholes. By the same token, when markets are all over the place, we return to our belief that over the long term, three prices tend to determine the long-term direction of asset prices. These three prices are the price of energy, the price of capital (as measured by the yield on 10-year US treasuries) and the price of the US dollar. Investors who get the direction of these three prices broadly right usually can call the direction of growth versus value, emerging markets versus developed markets, bonds versus equities versus commodities, etc… With that in mind, what does all of the above mean for the direction of the key three prices?
